title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases of the Supreme People's Court (2009)
keywords_en: Intellectual property; Supreme People's Court intellectual property case
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2009)

Fa [2010] No. 173

High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

In 2009, with the further improvement of the working mechanism for judicial protection of intellectual property rights and the implementation of the revised Civil Procedure Law, the number of intellectual property cases accepted and concluded by the Supreme People's Court rose sharply. There was an increase in new types of cases and significant, complex, and difficult cases; the professional and technical nature of cases intensified; and the proportion of foreign-related cases grew. Through the trial and adjudication of individual cases, the Supreme People's Court conducted in-depth research on new issues and new fields and provided timely responses. To summarize trial experience, strengthen trial supervision and guidance, and improve and unify the standards for the application of law, this Court decided to issue the "Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2009)."

Issuing the annual report on intellectual property cases is a concentrated display of typical cases tried by the Supreme People's Court itself, an exploration and attempt to innovate the method of trial guidance, and a significant measure to promote judicial transparency and accept supervision from all sectors. The "Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2009)" compiles 37 typical cases on which the Supreme People's Court has already reached final conclusions, involving 44 typical issues concerning the application of law. The interpretations of relevant legal issues in these individual cases have important guiding significance for intellectual property trial work.

The "Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2009)" is hereby issued to you for reference and use by people's courts at all levels in their intellectual property trial work.

The notice is hereby given.

April 14, 2010

Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2009)

Preface

In 2009, with the further improvement of the working mechanism for judicial protection of intellectual property rights and the implementation of the revised Civil Procedure Law, the number of intellectual property cases accepted by the Intellectual Property Division of the Supreme People's Court continued to grow, the number of concluded cases rose sharply, and the functions of the Supreme People's Court in trial supervision and professional guidance of intellectual property cases were effectively exercised.

In 2009, the Intellectual Property Division of the Supreme People's Court newly accepted a total of 297 intellectual property cases of various types. Together with 143 cases carried over from 2008, there were a total of 440 cases pending, an increase of 33.7% compared to 2008. Among the newly accepted cases, classified by the type of right involved, there were 121 patent cases, 61 trademark cases, 41 copyright cases, 10 trade secret cases, 9 other unfair competition cases, 7 intellectual property contract cases, 1 new plant variety case, and 47 advisory cases (mainly concerning the determination of jurisdiction over intellectual property cases). Classified by the trial procedure, there were 8 second instance cases, 230 cases applying for retrial, 12 cases directly retried by the Supreme People's Court, and 47 advisory cases. A total of 390 intellectual property cases of various types were concluded throughout the year, an increase of 111.96% compared to 2008. Among the concluded cases, there were 10 second instance cases, 319 cases applying for retrial, 14 cases directly retried by the Supreme People's Court, and 47 advisory cases. Among the concluded cases applying for retrial, 212 applications for retrial were dismissed by ruling, 12 cases were directly retried by ruling, 43 cases were remanded for retrial, 28 cases were withdrawn upon settlement, 21 cases were referred to the court of first instance for review by letter (concerning some administrative cases applying for retrial on intellectual property matters), and 3 cases were handled by other means.

The intellectual property cases tried by the Supreme People's Court in 2009 exhibited the following characteristics: an increase in new types of cases and significant, complex, and difficult cases, with growing social impact; an increase in the professional and technical nature of cases, making trial more difficult; and an increase in the proportion of foreign-related cases, attracting greater international attention. New, complex, and difficult cases constantly challenged the boundaries of the law, expanding new areas requiring legal regulation, and generating more and stronger new judicial demands. Through the trial and adjudication of individual cases, the Supreme People's Court conducted in-depth research on new issues and new fields and provided timely responses, thereby clarifying boundaries where the law was ambiguous, pointing the way at crossroads, and creating rules where there were gaps. These individual case adjudications reflect the creative efforts of the Supreme People's Court in maintaining harmony between stability and change in the law, balancing private interests and public interests, and achieving unity between legal effects and social effects. As the highest judicial organ of the state, the individual case adjudications of the Supreme People's Court can not only finally resolve disputes between the parties but also establish behavioral norms for the relevant public and the legality of enterprise competition models, and guide the development direction of industries and sectors, thereby continuously advancing the process of intellectual property rule of law in China through its unique constitutional status and judicial behavior.

Based on summarizing the experience of the Supreme People's Court's first issuance of the "Supreme People's Court Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (2008)" in 2009, this year the Supreme People's Court selected 37 typical cases with universal guiding significance from intellectual property cases on which it had already reached final conclusions, forming this annual report with a new writing style and publishing it to the public. It should be noted that although some cases, especially those intellectual property cases where the Supreme People's Court remanded for retrial by High People's Courts, are also typical, according to the provisions of relevant procedural laws, the Supreme People's Court did not make final conclusion statements on these cases; therefore, such cases are not included in this annual report.

I. Trial of Patent Cases

1. Whether an Inferior Technical Solution Falls Within the Scope of Protection of a Patent Right

In practice, there are situations where the alleged infringer omits or replaces a technical feature of the patented technical solution, resulting in a technical effect inferior to that of the patented technical solution. Whether such an inferior technical solution falls within the scope of protection of the patent right has given rise to two different opinions in past judicial practice. One opinion holds that if the inferior technical solution is clearly caused by the intentional omission or replacement of a certain technical feature, the doctrine of equivalents should be applied to find infringement. The other opinion holds that the determination of patent infringement should adhere to the principle of all technical features; if the inferior technical solution lacks a certain technical feature of the patented technical solution, or the corresponding technical features are neither identical nor equivalent, it should not be found to constitute infringement.

In the case of the retrial applicant Zhang Jianhua v. the respondent Shenyang Direct-Connected High-Rise Heating Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Direct-Connected Company) and the appellee at second instance Shenyang Gaolian High-Rise Heating Network Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Gaolian Company) - dispute over infringement of utility model patent [(2008) Min Ti Zi No. 83], the Supreme People's Court held that when a court determines whether an alleged infringing technical solution falls within the scope of protection of a patent right, it should compare the technical features of the alleged infringing technical solution with all the technical features recited in the patent claim; if the alleged infringing technical solution lacks a certain patented technical feature, resulting in an inferior technical effect, it should be determined that the alleged infringing technical solution does not fall within the scope of protection of the patent right.

The basic facts of the case are: Direct-Connected Company held the exclusive right to use two utility model patents, "Exhaust Break Device for Direct-Connected Heating of High-Rise Buildings Without Water Tanks" and "Rotational Resistance Device for Direct-Connected Heating System of High-Rise Buildings Without Water Tanks." Zhang Jianhua had previously worked at Direct-Connected Company, participating in the installation and maintenance of the break device and rotational resistance device, and shortly after leaving Direct-Connected Company, he established Gaolian Company. In August 2002, Direct-Connected Company sued Zhang Jianhua and Gaolian Company in the Shenyang Intermediate People's Court of Liaoning Province, alleging that the buffer and gas separator they produced and sold infringed the two patents in question. Upon comparison, the technical features of the break device patent and the alleged infringing buffer differed as follows: the alleged infringing product lacked the patent's surrounding threaded guide plate; the breathing device of the alleged infringing product was a check exhaust valve, which could only exhaust air but not inhale. The technical features of the rotational resistance device patent and the alleged infringing gas separator differed in that the alleged infringing product lacked a baffle plate and anti-spin plate, but was provided with a gas collection cover. The Shenyang Intermediate People's Court at first instance held that the break device patent was provided with a surrounding threaded guide plate, which strengthens water flow into a film flow state to achieve gas-water separation. The alleged infringing buffer, lacking the surrounding threaded guide plate, could not strengthen the formation of film flow motion, resulting in reduced effects of pressure reduction and speed reduction, and relative to the patented technical solution of the break device, it was an inferior technical solution. The break device patent uses a breathing device for regular inhalation and exhalation to maintain normal atmospheric pressure within the system, and achieves system sealing by water sealing to reduce system oxygen corrosion. The alleged infringing buffer was provided with a check exhaust valve; since the check exhaust valve could only exhaust but not inhale, when the system operation is unstable, especially when the pressure inside the buffer is less than atmospheric pressure, external air cannot enter, creating a vacuum inside the buffer, which not only prevents the formation of film flow motion but also renders the system inoperable. Compared with the breathing device of the break device patent, the check exhaust valve was an inferior technical feature. The alleged infringing gas separator lacked the anti-spin plate, and relying solely on the friction between the water flow and the return pipe wall for anti-spin effect was inferior to the anti-spin effect of the anti-spin plate, which was also an inferior change to the corresponding technical feature of the rotational resistance device patent. Since the patented technology was already publicly known, and Zhang Jianhua had previously worked at Direct-Connected Company, he could easily omit the essential technical features of the patent, and it was precisely because he omitted these essential technical features that the performance and effect of the alleged infringing technical solution were inferior; therefore, the alleged infringing technical solution fell within the scope of protection of the patent right, and Zhang Jianhua and Gaolian Company constituted patent infringement. Accordingly, the court ordered Gaolian Company and Zhang Jianhua to bear infringement liability. Zhang Jianhua, dissatisfied with the first instance judgment, appealed. The Liaoning High People's Court at second instance agreed with the first instance court's determination that the alleged infringing product constituted an inferior solution and constituted infringement by equivalents, and thus dismissed the appeal and affirmed the original judgment. Zhang Jianhua, dissatisfied with the second instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on July 24, 2009, to directly retry the case, and by retrial judgment on October 30, 2009, reversed the civil judgments of the first and second instances and dismissed Direct-Connected Company's claims.

The Supreme People's Court found during the retrial that when a court determines whether an alleged infringing technical solution falls within the scope of protection of a patent right, it should compare the technical features of the alleged infringing technical solution with all the technical features recited in the patent claim. If the alleged infringing technical solution lacks one or more technical features recited in the patent claim, or if one or more technical features of the alleged infringing technical solution are neither identical nor equivalent to the corresponding technical features recited in the patent claim, the court should determine that the alleged infringing technical solution does not fall within the scope of protection of the patent right. Whether the alleged infringing technical solution results in an inferior technical effect due to the lack of a certain patented technical feature is not a factor to be considered in the determination of patent infringement. In this case, the alleged infringing technical solution, lacking more than one technical feature of the patent, did not fall within the scope of protection of the patent right, and Zhang Jianhua and Gaolian Company did not constitute patent infringement.

2. Application of the Doctrine of Estoppel

The doctrine of estoppel means that a patent applicant or patentee, having surrendered a technical solution through amendments to the claims or specification or through statements made during patent grant or invalidation proceedings, cannot later assert that such technical solution be included within the scope of protection of the patent right in a patent infringement dispute. Where the alleged infringer does not plead the application of the doctrine of estoppel, whether a court may proactively apply the doctrine of estoppel is not explicitly stipulated by current laws and judicial interpretations.

In the case of the retrial applicant Shen Qiheng v. the respondent Shanghai Shengmao Traffic Facilities Engineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shengmao Company) - dispute over infringement of utility model patent [(2009) Min Shen Zi No. 239], the Supreme People's Court pointed out that even if the alleged infringer does not assert the application of the doctrine of estoppel, a court may, based on the facts already ascertained, apply the doctrine of estoppel to impose necessary limitations on the scope of equivalents.

The basic facts of the case are: On December 18, 2000, Shen Qiheng filed a utility model patent application entitled "Automobile Ground Lock" with the State Intellectual Property Office, which was granted on November 21, 2001. Claim 1 of the patent in question stated: "An automobile ground lock, characterized in that it consists of a base (1), a spindle (2), a movable post (3), and a lock (4), wherein the base (1) is fixed to the ground, the movable post (3) is connected to the base (1) through the spindle (2), and the movable post is provided with a hole for inserting the lock (4)." On March 19, 2003, a third party, Chuanyang Company, filed an invalidation request against the patent in question with the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office. The Patent Reexamination Board made Decision No. 6101, declaring Claim 1 invalid and maintaining the patent valid on the basis of Claims 2, 3, and 4. Shen Qiheng, dissatisfied with this decision, filed an administrative lawsuit, stating in his complaint: "The movable post is provided with a hole for inserting the lock. The meaning of this description is that the lock is not permanently fixed in the hole but exhibits two connection states depending on the usage condition, that is, when locked, it is located in the hole of the movable post, and when opened, it is taken out of the hole, separating from the hole of the movable post." On April 15, 2005, the Beijing High People's Court rendered Administrative Judgment (2005) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 37 (hereinafter referred to as Administrative Judgment No. 37), overturning Decision No. 6101. On March 15, 2006, the Patent Reexamination Board made Decision No. 8127 anew, maintaining the patent valid. Decision No. 8127 found: "When the ground lock is locked, the hole provided in the movable post of Claim 1 allows the entire lock to be inserted to achieve the purpose of locking the ground lock. When the ground lock is unlocked, the lock can be completely removed, and no additional fixing device is needed on the movable post to secure the lock. Therefore, this patent has substantive features and progress over the prior art... and possesses inventiveness." On September 26, 2006, Shen Qiheng sued in the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, alleging that the vehicle parking locks produced and sold by Shengmao Company fell within the scope of protection of the patent in question, and requested an order for Shengmao Company to cease infringement and compensate for losses. The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found that the lock of the alleged infringing product was fixed on the base, which differed from the "movable post provided with a hole for inserting the lock" in Claim 1, and according to the doctrine of estoppel, Shen Qiheng could not assert patent infringement based on equivalents, and dismissed Shen Qiheng's claims. The Shanghai High People's Court affirmed the first instance judgment upon second instance appeal. On January 9, 2009, Shen Qiheng applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On August 18, 2009, the Supreme People's Court ruled to reject Shen Qiheng's retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court reviewed and held that the doctrine of estoppel is a restriction on the finding of infringement by equivalents. To maintain a balance of interests between the patentee and the public, courts should not be restricted from proactively applying the doctrine of estoppel. Therefore, when determining whether infringement by equivalents exists, even if the alleged infringer does not assert the application of the doctrine of estoppel, a court may, based on the facts already ascertained, apply the doctrine of estoppel to impose necessary limitations on the scope of equivalents, so as to reasonably determine the scope of protection of the patent right.

3. Interpretation of the Sequence of Steps in a Method Patent Claim

A method patent is a technical solution for solving a particular technical problem, comprising a series of technological processes or operational steps. When a method patent claim does not explicitly define the sequence of steps, there is controversy over whether the sequence of steps imposes limitations on the scope of protection of the method patent.

In the case of the retrial applicant OBE-Factory, Ungerer & Baumgartner GmbH (hereinafter referred to as OBE Company) v. the respondent Zhejiang Kanghua Glasses Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kanghua Company) - dispute over infringement of invention patent [(2008) Min Shen Zi No. 980], the Supreme People's Court held that when applying the doctrine of equivalents to determine infringement in a method patent case, a court may, in conjunction with the patent specification and drawings, the prosecution history, the overall technical solution recited in the claims, and the logical relationship between the various steps, determine whether each step should be performed in a specific sequence; both the steps themselves and the order of performing the steps should impose limitations on the scope of protection of the method patent.

The basic facts of the case are: On April 24, 1996, OBE Company filed an invention patent application entitled "Method for Manufacturing a Spring Hinge" with the State Intellectual Property Office, which was granted on October 24, 2001. Claim 1 of the patent in question stated: "1. A method for manufacturing a spring hinge, which hinge consists of at least one housing, one hinge member, and one spring, characterized in that the method comprises the steps of: providing a metal strip for forming the hinge member; cutting out an area substantially consistent with the outline of the hinge member; forming a circular portion by stamping to form the shoulder of the hinge member; punching out the hinge hole of the hinge member." On June 24, 2002, OBE Company sued, alleging that Kanghua Company, without its permission, manufactured, used, offered for sale, and sold spring hinge products falling within the scope of protection of the patent in question for business purposes, constituting patent infringement, and requested an order for Kanghua Company to cease infringement and bear civil liability such as compensation for losses. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found that Kanghua Company's process for processing the hinge member was: 1. Manually feeding the metal strip into a punching machine to punch out the hinge member; 2. Manually clamping the front part of the hinge member with pliers and using a forging machine to hammer the rear part of the hinge member round; 3. Manually clamping the front part of the hinge member with pliers and inserting the hinge member into a punching machine to punch the hole; 4. Manually threading a lead wire through the round hole at the front part of the hinge member, stringing several hinge members together, and then polishing with a polishing wheel. The court held that Claim 1 of the patent comprised four steps, and Kanghua Company's processing steps were also four. Although the order of die forging and punching could be adjusted, the adjustment did not produce a new effect. Kanghua Company's method was equivalent to the method protected by Claim 1 and fell within the scope of protection of the patent in question. The Beijing High People's Court at second instance held that, according to the description of the patent specification, the patented technical solution was achieved when the steps were performed sequentially; changing the sequence could not achieve the technical effect and technical purpose of the patented method. Kanghua Company's manufacturing method comprised four steps, among which the order of rounding and punching could be adjusted, which differed from the method of sequentially performing the steps in the patent solution. The manufacturing method of the alleged infringing product was neither identical nor equivalent to the patented method and did not fall within the scope of protection of the patent in question. Thus, the second instance judgment reversed the first instance judgment and dismissed OBE Company's claims. OBE Company, dissatisfied with the second instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on August 29, 2009, to reject its retrial application.

4. Trial Approach and Technical Comparison Analysis Method in Patent Infringement Cases

Patent infringement cases, due to the involvement of examination and judgment of professional technical facts and technical comparison analysis, have certain regularity and particularity in the trial approach, analysis and comparison, and even the expression of judicial documents. Although the current judicial practice in determining patent infringement generally follows a basic model of examination, analysis, and reasoning, there are still considerable differences across regions in the analysis of certain specific issues and the expression of judicial documents.

In the case of the reapplicant Xue Shengguo v. the respondents Zhao Xiangmin and Zhao Zhangren regarding a dispute over utility model patent infringement [(2009) Minshen Zi No. 1562], the Supreme People's Court conducted an in-depth analysis on how to specifically determine the "three basic similarities" and "obviousness" when applying the doctrine of equivalents. The Supreme People's Court also pointed out that if the patentee's explanation of a technical feature during the patent infringement proceedings does not exceed the scope of the claims and is consistent with the patent specification and drawings, that explanation may be used to define the technical feature.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: On August 8, 2007, Xue Shengguo filed a patent infringement lawsuit against Zhao Xiangmin and Zhao Zhangren. Xue Shengguo's patent claim reads: "A dough kneading machine for vermicelli processing, comprising: a frame (1), a drive motor (2) disposed on said frame (1), characterized in that: a hopper (5) with an inlet and an outlet (3, 4) is provided on the upper part of the frame (1), and a conveying auger (6) driven by said drive motor (2) is horizontally arranged in said hopper (5); two interconnected U-shaped kneading troughs (7, 8) are arranged side by side on the frame (1) above said outlet (4), the bottom of one U-shaped kneading trough (7) communicating with said outlet (4); and a kneading hammer (9, 10) is respectively provided on the frame (1) above each U-shaped kneading trough (7, 8), the support frame (11) of said two kneading hammers (9, 10) being connected to the power shaft of the drive motor (2) via a crank-link mechanism (12)." The Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court of Henan Province held at first instance that the technical features of the allegedly infringing product were not identical to the essential technical features of the patent and did not fall within the scope of protection of Xue Shengguo's patent, thus determining no infringement, and dismissed Xue Shengguo's claims. After Xue Shengguo appealed, the Henan High People's Court held at second instance that the first instance judgment's finding that some technical features were identical or equivalent was improper, but the conclusion that the allegedly infringing product did not fall within the scope of protection of Xue Shengguo's patent and thus did not constitute infringement was correct, and therefore dismissed the appeal and affirmed the original judgment. Xue Shengguo, still dissatisfied, applied for retrial to the Supreme People's Court. After review through a hearing, the Supreme People's Court also concluded that the respondents did not constitute patent infringement, but for reasons different from those of the original courts. The Supreme People's Court ruled on November 26, 2009 to reject Xue Shengguo's retrial application.

Based on the decomposition and determination of the six corresponding technical features between the patented technical solution and the allegedly infringing product, the Supreme People's Court held that, for the fifth corresponding technical feature, the allegedly infringing product merely moved the hopper upward relative to the kneading troughs on the basis of the patent, thereby utilizing the gravity of the dough itself. However, due to the inherent low fluidity of the dough, without using the conveying auger to squeeze it, it would be difficult to achieve the purpose of conveying the dough from the hopper to the kneading trough by relying solely on the dough's own gravity. Conversely, if the dough's own gravity alone could achieve the self-flow of the dough from the hopper to the kneading trough, there would be no need to adopt the technical means of the conveying auger. Therefore, the allegedly infringing product essentially still uses the conveying auger to squeeze the dough through the outlet into the kneading trough, which is the same as the patent; both require the conveying auger to realize the function of squeezing and conveying the dough from the hopper to the kneading trough. It can be seen that compared with this technical feature of the patent, the allegedly infringing product adopts substantially the same means, achieves substantially the same function, and obtains substantially the same effect. Moreover, the fact that an object can slide down from top to bottom due to its own gravity is common knowledge. Therefore, moving the hopper upward relative to the kneading troughs would be conceivable to a person of ordinary skill in the relevant technical field without the need for creative labor. In accordance with the relevant provisions of the judicial interpretation on patents, this technical feature of the allegedly infringing product constitutes an equivalent feature of the corresponding patented technical feature. Regarding the sixth patented technical feature, the patentee expressly confirmed that the two kneading hammers share a common support frame, which is connected to the power shaft of the drive motor via a crank-link mechanism, and the power drive device drives the two kneading hammers to reciprocate upward and downward in the same direction through the crank-link mechanism. The patentee's explanation of this technical feature does not exceed the scope of the corresponding technical content recorded in the claims and is consistent with the relative positions and connection relationships among the two kneading hammers, the support frame, the crank-link mechanism, and the drive motor as shown in the patent specification and drawings. Therefore, the essential technical feature 6 of Xue Shengguo's patent at issue can be defined as: a kneading hammer is respectively provided on the frame above each U-shaped kneading trough, the two kneading hammers share a common support frame connected to the power shaft of the drive motor via a crank-link mechanism, and the power drive device drives the two kneading hammers to reciprocate upward and downward in the same direction through the crank-link mechanism. Comparing the sixth corresponding technical feature, in the patent, the two kneading hammers share one support frame, and the power drive device drives the two kneading hammers to reciprocate upward and downward in the same direction through the crank-link mechanism; in the allegedly infringing product, each kneading hammer has its own support frame, and the support frames of the two kneading hammers are connected by a lever, with the support frame of one kneading hammer being driven by the power drive device through a crank-link mechanism, causing the two kneading hammers to reciprocate upward and downward in opposite directions. Although both have the basic function of supporting the kneading hammers with the support frame and driving the support frame to move up and down via the crank-link mechanism, from the perspective of the working principle and motion mode of the kneading hammers, it is clear that different technical means are adopted and should not be considered as substantially the same means. Moreover, because the power drive device in the allegedly infringing product drives the support frame of only one kneading hammer, while the device in the patent drives the support frame of two kneading hammers, the design of the allegedly infringing product saves more kinetic energy and can use a relatively smaller power drive motor. Furthermore, the allegedly infringing product's use of the lever principle to make the two kneading hammers reciprocate in opposite directions also avoids the useless work done when the two kneading hammers in the patent move upward in the same direction with a shared support frame. Thus, there is also a significant difference in technical effect. In addition, this changed means in the allegedly infringing product would not be conceivable to a person of ordinary skill in the relevant technical field without creative labor. Therefore, the corresponding technical features of the two are neither identical nor equivalent. Since the allegedly infringing product has at least one corresponding technical feature that is neither identical nor equivalent compared to the Xue Shengguo patent at issue, the allegedly infringing product does not fall within the scope of protection of the Xue Shengguo patent.

5. Interpretation of "Declared Invalid Patent Right" under Article 47(1) of the Patent Law

Article 47(1) of the Patent Law provides that a patent right that has been declared invalid shall be deemed to have never existed from the beginning. The decision of the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office declaring a patent right invalid is a neutral ruling made in response to a dispute between the requester for invalidation and the patentee regarding the validity of the patent right. Although such an invalidation decision has the authoritative nature of an administrative act, its effect is not finally determined because it may be subject to administrative litigation. When a court hearing a patent infringement case learns that the Patent Reexamination Board has made a decision declaring the patent right invalid, there are different practices regarding whether to suspend the infringement proceedings or directly dismiss the plaintiff's claims based on the invalidation decision.

In the case of the reapplicant Shenzhen Wanhong Technology Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Wanhong Company) v. the respondents Shenzhen Pingzhi Dongfang Technology Development Co., Ltd., Xin Nuoyazhou Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., and Chuangxin Nuoyazhou Electronics (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. regarding a dispute over infringement of utility model patent [(2009) Minshen Zi No. 1573], the Supreme People's Court held that the "declared invalid patent right" in Article 47(1) of the Patent Law refers to a patent right that has been declared invalid by a final and conclusive decision on the invalidation request review made by the Patent Reexamination Board. Before the effect of such invalidation decision becomes final and conclusive, it is not appropriate to directly base a judgment on it to dismiss the right holder's claims.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: Wanhong Company filed a utility model patent infringement lawsuit against Shenzhen Pingzhi Dongfang Technology Development Co., Ltd., Xin Nuoyazhou Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., and Chuangxin Nuoyazhou Electronics (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. on October 25, 2008. The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province rendered a first-instance judgment on February 25, 2009, finding the three defendants liable for infringement. The three defendants appealed. During the second instance, the Guangdong High People's Court ascertained that the Patent Reexamination Board had issued Invalidation Decision No. 13590 on June 24, 2009, declaring the utility model patent at issue entirely invalid. Wanhong Company applied for a suspension of the proceedings on the grounds that the patentee had filed an administrative lawsuit against the above decision. The Guangdong High People's Court, on the grounds that the utility model patent at issue had been declared entirely invalid, rendered a judgment setting aside the first-instance judgment and dismissing all of Wanhong Company's claims. Dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, Wanhong Company applied for retrial to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ascertained that the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court had decided on July 2, 2009 to accept the administrative lawsuit filed by the patentee against Invalidation Decision No. 13590, and that the administrative case had not yet been concluded by the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on December 8, 2009 to instruct the Guangdong High People's Court to retry the case.

The Supreme People's Court held that, for a decision of the Patent Reexamination Board declaring a patent right invalid, if the party concerned fails to file a lawsuit with the People's Court within three months from the date of receipt of the notice, the effect of the decision becomes final and conclusive. If the party concerned has filed an administrative lawsuit in accordance with the law, the effect of the decision becomes final and conclusive only after the decision is upheld as lawful and valid by an effective administrative judgment. In this case, although the patent at issue was declared entirely invalid by Invalidation Decision No. 13590 of the Patent Reexamination Board, the patentee had filed an administrative lawsuit against that decision within the statutory period, and the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court had accepted the case, so the effect of the decision was obviously not final and conclusive. Under these circumstances, Wanhong Company applied for a suspension of the proceedings. The second-instance court's direct dismissal of all of Wanhong Company's claims based on the fact that the patent at issue had been declared entirely invalid by Invalidation Decision No. 13590 constituted an error in the application of law.

6. Retroactive Effect of a Decision Declaring a Patent Right Invalid

Article 47(2) of the Patent Law (as amended for the second time in 2000) provides: "The decision declaring a patent right invalid shall have no retroactive effect on any judgment or order on patent infringement that has been rendered and enforced by the People's Court before the declaration of invalidity, on any decision concerning the handling of patent infringement disputes that has been performed or compulsorily executed, or on any patent exploitation license contract and patent assignment contract that have been performed prior to the declaration of invalidity. However, compensation shall be made for losses caused to others by the patentee's bad faith." During the trial of civil cases, the People's Court may make multiple orders on procedural matters to ensure the smooth progress of the trial. Not all such orders are immune from the effect of a decision declaring a patent right invalid.

In the case of the reapplicant Anji Xueqiang Bamboo Wood Products Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Xueqiang Company) v. the respondent Xu Zanyou regarding a dispute over other infringement [(2008) Minshen Zi No. 762], the Supreme People's Court clarified the scope of "orders" under Article 47(2) of the Patent Law (as amended for the second time in 2000).

The basic facts of this case are as follows: On June 13, 2001, Xu Zanyou applied to the State Intellectual Property Office for a design patent titled "Carpet (Bamboo)," which was granted on March 6, 2002. In March 2004, the Hangzhou Customs and Shanghai Customs, at the request of Xu Zanyou, detained containers of export products belonging to Xueqiang Company on suspicion of infringement of the patent at issue. On April 2, 2004, Xu Zanyou filed a lawsuit with the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province, accusing Xueqiang Company of infringing the patent at issue, and applied for a court order to detain the goods in the above containers. At the same time, Xu Zanyou demanded that Xueqiang Company remove the products suspected of infringing the patent at issue from exhibitions in Shanghai, Guangzhou, and other places. On May 1, 2004, Xueqiang Company filed a request with the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office to declare the patent at issue invalid. On August 18, 2005, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Invalidation Decision No. 7432, declaring the patent at issue entirely invalid. On September 15, 2005, Xueqiang Company filed a lawsuit with the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court, alleging that Xu Zanyou's application for property preservation measures was erroneous, causing significant economic losses and adverse social impact, and requested that Xu Zanyou be ordered to compensate for losses, eliminate the impact, make an apology, and bear all litigation costs. The Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Xu Zanyou's actions of applying for customs detention, court seizure, and requesting Xueqiang Company to remove the suspected infringing products from exhibitions before the patent at issue was declared invalid were lawful. After the patent was declared invalid, Xueqiang Company's claim for compensation for losses and a public apology from Xu Zanyou for the above actions was without sufficient basis, and thus dismissed Xueqiang Company's claims. After appeal, the Zhejiang High People's Court held at second instance that Xueqiang Company failed to prove that Xu Zanyou acted with bad faith when carrying out the above actions, and since the above actions were completed before the patent at issue was declared invalid, pursuant to Article 47(2) of the Patent Law, the decision declaring the patent at issue invalid had no retroactive effect on those actions. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed. Dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, Xueqiang Company applied for retrial to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on March 24, 2009 to instruct the Zhejiang High People's Court to retry the case.

The Supreme People's Court held that the "orders" referred to in Article 47(2) of the Patent Law (as amended for the second time in 2000) mean orders related to patent infringement, i.e., orders made and enforced in a case where the People's Court has rendered an effective judgment finding patent infringement. This does not include orders involved in cases where the judgment finds no patent infringement. Since the patent at issue was declared invalid by the Patent Reexamination Board, the trial court rendered a judgment finding that Xueqiang Company did not infringe the patent. Therefore, the earlier property preservation orders made by the trial court in this case do not fall within the scope of "orders" under Article 47(2) of the Patent Law, and the decision declaring the patent at issue invalid has retroactive effect on them. Similarly, the decision declaring the patent at issue invalid also has retroactive effect on Xu Zanyou's actions of applying for customs detention and requesting the alleged infringer to remove exhibits. The patentee's exercise of the right to sue and apply for relevant measures in accordance with the patent law is a right granted by law. However, when exercising their rights, patentees must not harm the lawful rights and interests of others. Since the stability of a patent right is relative, anyone can file a request to declare an already granted patent invalid through the invalidation procedure. The patentee should be aware of the possibility that their patent right may be declared invalid. Therefore, when exercising relevant rights, especially measures such as applying for property preservation or ordering cessation of relevant acts that may directly cause harm to the respondent, the patentee should exercise caution and fully assess the litigation risks. Xu Zanyou failed to fulfill the duty of care. Without finally confirming that Xueqiang Company infringed the patent at issue, he applied for measures such as property preservation and orders to cease relevant acts that directly caused harm to Xueqiang Company, which constituted an erroneous application and an infringement.

II. Trial of Copyright Cases

7. Presumed Ownership of Works Made for Hire

According to Article 16(2) of the Copyright Law, the ownership of copyright in works made for hire may be agreed upon by contract, but this provision does not specify the specific form of such contractual agreement.

In the case of the reapplicant Chen Junfeng v. the respondent Jindun Publishing House regarding a dispute over copyright infringement [(2009) Minjian Zi No. 361], the Supreme People's Court, based on the conduct of both parties, presumed that the parties intended the copyright in the work at issue to belong to Jindun Publishing House, thereby affirming that the ownership of copyright in works made for hire may be determined by presumption.

8. Statutory license for making sound recordings using musical works that have been lawfully recorded as sound recordings, and copying and distributing them

Article 39, paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law stipulates the statutory license system for producers of sound recordings to use musical works that have been lawfully recorded as sound recordings to make sound recordings. According to this provision, a producer of sound recordings may, without permission from the copyright owner, use a musical work that has been lawfully recorded as a sound recording to make a sound recording, provided that remuneration is paid in accordance with the provisions; if the copyright owner declares that use is not permitted, such use shall not be made. At the same time, Article 41, paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law provides that a licensee who reproduces, distributes, or communicates to the public via information networks sound or video recordings shall also obtain permission from the copyright owner and the performer, and pay remuneration. The Copyright Law does not clarify the relationship between these two provisions. In this regard, some opinions hold that after a producer of sound recordings uses a musical work that has been lawfully recorded as a sound recording to make a sound recording, the reproduction and distribution of the sound recording still require permission from the copyright owner of the musical work, i.e., Article 41, paragraph 2 restricts Article 39, paragraph 3.

In the retrial judgment of the case of the applicant for retrial Guangdong Dasheng Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Dasheng Company) v. Wang Haicheng, Wang Haixing, and Wang Haiyan (hereinafter referred to as Wang Haicheng et al.), and the defendants at first instance Chongqing Sanxia Optical Disc Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sanxia Company), Jiujiang Liansheng Plaza Supermarket Co., Ltd., and Nanchang Department Store Co., Ltd. — dispute over copyright infringement [(2008) Min Ti Zi No. 57, hereinafter referred to as the "Dasheng Company Case"], the Supreme People's Court clarified the legal application relationship between Article 39, paragraph 3 and Article 41, paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law, confirming that once a sound recording of a musical work made with the permission of the copyright owner is made public, the use of the musical work by others to make another sound recording and copy or distribute it shall be governed by the statutory license provided in Article 39, paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law, and the provision of "with the permission of the copyright owner" in Article 41, paragraph 2 shall no longer apply.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: "Yakxi" is a musical work adapted and lyrics written by Wang Luobin in 1957 based on a Turpan folk song. After Wang Luobin's death, his son Wang Haicheng and others authorized the Music Copyright Society of China (hereinafter referred to as the "MCSC") to manage the rights of public performance, broadcasting, and recording and distribution of the musical work. In 2004, Luo Lin (stage name Daolang) entered into a contract with Dasheng Company, under which Dasheng Company obtained the right to produce, publish, and distribute sound recordings (CDs) of the singing music album program "Kashgar Populus" produced by Luo Lin, who held the copyright. Thereafter, Dasheng Company entered into a contract with Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House, agreeing that the latter would produce, publish, and distribute the aforementioned album recordings. Dasheng Company also entered into a contract with Sanxia Company for entrusted reproduction and processing, agreeing to reproduce 200,000 copies of the recordings. On December 8, 2004, Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House commissioned Sanxia Company to reproduce 900,000 copies. Subsequently, Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House applied to the MCSC for the use of the musical works "Snow Lotus on the Ice Mountain," "Beat the Drum and Sing," and "Yakxi" to produce and distribute 200,000 copies of the "Kashgar Populus" album recordings, with a wholesale price of RMB 6.5, and paid the MCSC a usage fee of RMB 21,900 for the three musical works, for which the MCSC issued a fee certificate. Wang Haicheng et al. sued, claiming that the defendant's unauthorized reproduction and distribution of the infringing discs violated their reproduction and distribution rights, and sought an order to stop the infringement, compensate for losses, and make an apology. The Intermediate People's Court of Jiujiang City, Jiangxi Province, held at first instance that the musical work "Yakxi" had been publicly published and recorded as a sound recording long before the reproduction and distribution of the recordings in question. Pursuant to Article 39, paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law, the use of the musical work by Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House and Dasheng Company to make sound recordings constituted a statutory license, and permission from the copyright owner was not required, but remuneration should be paid. Wang Haicheng et al. had entrusted the management of the musical work to the MCSC on a trust basis, and the MCSC had the right to license its use to others. Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House, Dasheng Company, and Sanxia Company fell within the scope of statutory license use. Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House paid remuneration to the copyright owner based on 200,000 copies, but failed to pay remuneration for the additional 700,000 copies in accordance with the provisions, thereby infringing upon Wang Haicheng et al.'s right to remuneration. In accordance with the "Interim Provisions on the Standard for Remuneration for Statutory License of Sound Recordings" formulated by the National Copyright Administration in August 1993, the amount of compensation was determined as twice the wholesale price of the recordings (RMB 6.5 x 3.5% x 700,000 copies), totaling RMB 318,500. Sanxia Company did not constitute infringement of the copyright of the musical work. Dasheng Company and Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, filed an appeal. The High People's Court of Jiangxi Province held at second instance that, according to Article 41, paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law, to reproduce, publish, or distribute sound recordings, in addition to obtaining permission from the performer and paying remuneration, permission from the copyright owner of the musical work must also be obtained and remuneration paid. The MCSC's licensing and fee collection were rights exercised in relation to the use of musical works to make sound recordings, and did not constitute the exercise of the copyright owner's right to license and receive remuneration for the reproduction and distribution of sound recordings. The first-instance court's determination of the compensation amount for one musical work by doubling the total remuneration of all works contained in the entire recording lacked reasonableness. The court therefore vacated the first-instance judgment and ordered Dasheng Company and Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House to jointly compensate Wang Haicheng et al. RMB 150,000. Dasheng Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court decided to bring the case up for trial and, on March 6, 2009, issued a retrial judgment, vacating the first-instance and second-instance judgments and ordering Dasheng Company, Guangzhou Audio-Visual Publishing House, and Sanxia Company to pay Wang Haicheng et al. a usage fee of RMB 14,477 for the musical work.

The Supreme People's Court held in the retrial that Article 39, paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law establishes a statutory license system that restricts the rights of copyright owners of musical works. Although this paragraph only provides that making sound recordings using musical works that have been lawfully recorded as sound recordings by others may be done without the permission of the copyright owner, the legislative intent of this paragraph is to facilitate and promote the dissemination of musical works. Therefore, the reproduction and distribution of sound recordings made using such musical works should also be governed by this provision, and Article 41, paragraph 2 should not apply. Accordingly, once a sound recording of a musical work made with the permission of the copyright owner is made public, others using that musical work to make another sound recording and copying or distributing it do not need to obtain permission from the copyright owner of the musical work, but must pay remuneration to the copyright owner in accordance with the law. Given that the musical work "Yakxi" used in the album in question had been made into sound recordings by others on multiple occasions and widely disseminated before the album's release, and the copyright owner had not declared that use was not permitted, the defendant's use of the musical work to make, reproduce, and distribute the album recordings in question complied with the statutory license provisions and did not constitute infringement.

9. Direct infringement liability of internet service providers providing linking services

If an internet service provider uses the internet to directly infringe upon the copyright of others, it shall bear direct infringement liability for its actions. At the same time, Article 23 of the Regulations on the Protection of the Right to Communicate to the Public via Information Networks establishes a limitation of liability for internet service providers. This article provides that an internet service provider that provides search or linking services for service objects shall not bear liability for damages if, upon receiving a notice from the right holder, it disconnects the link to the infringing work, performance, or sound or video recording in accordance with the provisions of these Regulations. In judicial practice, internet service providers often claim that they are providing linking services and, after receiving the notice from the right holder, have already disconnected the link, and therefore should not bear liability for damages. Thus, determining whether an internet service provider is indeed providing linking services becomes the key to whether it should bear direct infringement liability.

In the case of the applicant for retrial Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ciwen Company) v. the respondent China Network Communications Group Corporation Hainan Branch (hereinafter referred to as Hainan Netcom Company) — dispute over copyright infringement [(2009) Min Ti Zi No. 17], the Supreme People's Court clarified the conditions under which an internet service provider providing network linking services bears direct infringement liability. From the retrial judgment in this case, it can be seen that if an internet service provider claiming to provide linking services provides the so-called linked webpage or website to the public as its own content, and the linked webpage or website does not display any corresponding domain name or website name information indicating that the webpage belongs to a third party, then it cannot be determined that the internet service provider is providing linking services, and it shall bear direct infringement liability for the allegedly infringing acts on that webpage or website.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Ciwen Company held the copyright to the film "Seven Swords" in mainland China. Hainan Netcom Company set up a "Movie Channel" on the homepage of its website www.hai169.com. Clicking on it entered "Movie World" (IP address 221.11.132.112), where the film could be watched online. Ciwen Company filed a lawsuit in the Haikou Intermediate People's Court of Hainan Province for copyright infringement, seeking an order to stop the infringement and compensate for losses. In the first-instance proceedings, Hainan Netcom Company submitted evidence showing that clicking the "Movie Channel" on its website's homepage led to "116 Daily Online" rather than the original "Movie World" webpage. The Haikou Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Hainan Netcom Company was providing linking services, had disconnected the link after being sued for infringement, and therefore should not bear infringement liability. The court dismissed Ciwen Company's claims. After an appeal, the High People's Court of Hainan Province upheld the first-instance judgment. Ciwen Company applied for retrial, and the Supreme People's Court decided to bring the case up for trial and issued a retrial judgment, vacating the first-instance and second-instance judgments and ordering Hainan Netcom Company to pay Ciwen Company RMB 80,000 as compensation for economic losses and reasonable expenses incurred for the litigation.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that clicking the "Movie Channel" on the homepage of Hainan Netcom's website led to a page where the film "Seven Swords" could be watched. Although the accessed page was named "Movie World," it did not display any corresponding domain name or website name information indicating that the webpage belonged to a third party, and the IP address of the webpage could not prove that the webpage belonged to another entity. This situation differs from what is commonly understood as a link; at least superficially, the webpage belonged to Hainan Netcom Company. If Hainan Netcom Company wished to prove that the webpage was a linked third-party website for which it should not bear liability for the infringing acts on that webpage, it should have submitted corresponding evidence. Since the IP address of the webpage fell within the range of addresses managed by Hainan Netcom Company, Hainan Netcom Company was able to provide such evidence, whereas the public, including Ciwen Company, could not obtain it. In the absence of relevant evidence submitted by Hainan Netcom Company, its defense that it merely provided linking services could not be sustained, and it should bear corresponding legal liability for the infringing act of playing the film to which Ciwen Company held copyright on that webpage. Even if the webpage indeed belonged to or was actually operated by a third party, since the "Movie Channel" was listed alongside Hainan Netcom Company's website "Homepage," "News Channel," "Literature Channel," etc., Hainan Netcom Company provided the webpage content to the public as one of its content channels. Moreover, from the notarial certificate submitted by Hainan Netcom Company in the original trial, which showed that the content of the "Movie Channel" was changed after being sued, it can be seen that the choice was entirely made independently by Hainan Netcom Company. Therefore, this conduct differs from an ordinary link pointing to a third-party website. Hainan Netcom Company should at least have conducted a certain level of review of the qualifications of the actual owner or operator of the website. In this case, Hainan Netcom Company to this day claims it does not know the actual operator of the webpage, which shows that it failed to fulfill even the minimum duty of care, and thus should also bear joint liability for the infringing acts occurring on that webpage.

III. Trademark Case Adjudication

(A) Adjudication of Administrative Cases on Trademark Authorization and Confirmation

10. Criteria for determining and applying the principle of "res judicata"

According to Article 35 of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law, where the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board has already made a ruling or decision on a trademark review application, no one may file a review application again on the same facts and grounds. This is the so-called principle of "res judicata."

In the case of the complainant Foshan Shengfang (United) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shengfang Company) v. the respondent Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board) and the third party at first instance Johnson & Johnson — administrative dispute over trademark [(2008) Xing Ti Zi No. 2, hereinafter referred to as the "Caile" trademark administrative case], the Supreme People's Court clarified the criteria for determining and applying the principle of "res judicata."

The basic facts of the case are as follows: On January 30, 1993, Johnson & Johnson was registered with the trademark No. 627498 for the handwritten traditional Chinese characters "Caile" (the cited trademark), with designated goods in Class 5 "Topical human antimicrobial agents." After July 1994, the non-party Xi'an Janssen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., with the permission of Johnson & Johnson, used the cited trademark on the drug "Ketoconazole Lotion" for the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis and scalp eczema. The disputed trademark was trademark No. 1214187 "Caile CAILE" held by Shengfang Company, filed on August 6, 1997, and registered on October 14, 1998, with designated goods in Class 3, including soap, cleaning preparations, shampoo, hair conditioner, facial cleanser, bath lotion, toothpaste, cosmetics, etc. In November 1998 and July 2000, Johnson & Johnson twice applied to the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board for cancellation of the disputed trademark registration. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board issued final rulings in December 1999 and September 2001, respectively, finding that the grounds raised by Johnson & Johnson could not be established and maintaining the registration of the disputed trademark. On August 20, 2002, Johnson & Johnson filed a third application with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to cancel the disputed trademark, on the grounds that the disputed trademark and the cited trademark constituted similar trademarks on similar goods, that the disputed trademark was a malicious imitation and copy of its well-known trademark, and that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Articles 13, 28, 31, and 41 of the current Trademark Law. On June 23, 2005, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board issued a ruling (Shang Ping Zi [2005] No. 1801) finding the cited trademark to be a well-known trademark and determining that the registration of the disputed trademark constituted a reproduction or imitation of another's well-known trademark on non-similar goods, misleading the public, and therefore canceled the registration of the disputed trademark. Shengfang Company, dissatisfied with the ruling, filed a lawsuit. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Johnson & Johnson submitted new evidence in this review application, which did not constitute a review application on the same facts and grounds. Therefore, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's acceptance of this dispute application did not violate legal procedures, and the court upheld the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's Ruling No. 1801. Shengfang Company appealed. The Beijing High People's Court held at second instance that Johnson & Johnson's application was based on the provisions of Article 13, paragraph 2 of the amended Trademark Law and submitted new evidence adding new facts. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board did not violate the principle of "res judicata." The court therefore sustained the first-instance judgment. Dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, Shengfang Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court decided to bring the case up for trial and, on October 22, 2009, issued a retrial judgment, vacating the original judgments and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's Ruling No. 1801.

The Supreme People's Court held in the retrial that when Johnson & Johnson filed the two previous review applications, it invoked Articles 17 and 27 of the pre-amendment Trademark Law, and Article 25(2) of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law, among other provisions, particularly those concerning well-known trademarks or marks with a high reputation, arguing that the disputed trademark was a malicious copy and imitation of a well-known trademark, that the disputed trademark and the cited trademark constituted similar marks on similar goods, and were likely to cause confusion, thereby exhausting all relevant legal grounds and bases that could be asserted at the time. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board (TRAB) had conducted substantive examination of the relevant facts and grounds, and twice ruled to maintain the registration of the disputed trademark. Johnson & Johnson invoked the amended Trademark Law, still using the well-known status of the trademark as the primary ground to apply for cancellation of the disputed trademark. The TRAB's acceptance and issuance of a ruling to cancel the disputed trademark in this review violated the principle of "ne bis in idem" (res judicata). Even if examined under the amended Trademark Law and its implementing regulations, the TRAB's current review ruling lacked a legal basis. Pursuant to Article 35 of the current Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law, for trademark disputes that have already been finally adjudicated, the TRAB may accept a new review application only if there are new facts or new grounds. New facts should be facts proven by new evidence, and new evidence should be evidence discovered after the original ruling or decision, or evidence that could not be obtained due to objective reasons or could not be submitted within the prescribed time limit during the original administrative procedure. If evidence that could have been submitted in the previous administrative procedure is accepted as new evidence, the legal restrictions on initiating administrative procedures would be rendered meaningless, which is detrimental to the formation of a stable legal order. The evidence submitted by Johnson & Johnson in this review application to prove that its cited trademark was well-known before the filing date of the disputed trademark does not constitute new evidence in the legal sense. The amendment of the law after the administrative ruling was made cannot constitute a new ground.

11. The retroactive effect of the Trademark Law (2001 Amendment) on trademark disputes that had already been subject to a final administrative ruling before the law came into effect

In the aforementioned "Cai Le" trademark administrative case, the Supreme People's Court also clarified the issue of the retroactive effect of the Trademark Law (2001 Amendment) on trademark disputes that had already been subject to a final administrative ruling before the law came into effect. In its judgment in that case, the Supreme People's Court held, based on the principle of protecting legitimate expectations, that the amended Trademark Law of 2001 does not have retroactive effect on trademark disputes that were already bound by a final ruling before the amendment.

The Supreme People's Court pointed out in the retrial judgment that the trademark dispute in question had already been subject to a final ruling before the Trademark Law (2001 Amendment) came into effect, and thus did not fall within the circumstances stipulated in Article 5 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Issues Concerning Jurisdiction over and Application of Law in the Trial of Trademark Cases, and the provisions of that judicial interpretation should not apply. Since the pre-amendment Trademark Law adopted a system of final administrative adjudication for trademark review, for disputed matters that had already received a final ruling at that time, the legal system then in force must be respected and maintained, and procedures cannot be reopened on the grounds that the amended law contains new provisions. Under the system of final administrative adjudication, a final ruling creates a stable order and generates reliance interests. The substantial use and promotion of the trademark by Shengfang Company after the final ruling, and the commercial reputation thus established, should be protected by law. The TRAB and the lower courts erred in law by determining that Johnson & Johnson's invocation of the amended Trademark Law constituted a new ground for filing the current review application, and by relying on Article 13(2) of the amended Trademark Law to cancel the disputed trademark.

12. Consideration of specific historical factors when determining trademark similarity

Trademark similarity means that the shape, pronunciation, meaning of the characters, or the composition and colors of the design, or the overall structure of the elements of two trademarks are similar, such that it is likely to cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or to believe there is a specific connection. When making this determination, the standard of attention of the relevant public should be used. Both overall comparison and comparison of the main parts should be conducted, and the distinctiveness and reputation of the prior registered trademark should be considered.

In the case of Hou Yong, the applicant for retrial, v. Harbin Qiulin Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Qiulin Group) and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, a trademark administrative dispute [2009] Zhixing Zi No. 15, the Supreme People's Court further pointed out that when applying the above method to determine trademark similarity, factors such as specific historical relationships and being in the same geographical area may also be considered, to assess whether the coexistence of the two trademarks is likely to cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or to believe there is a specific connection between them.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: In 1900, a Russian named Ivan Yakovlevich Qiulin (also referred to as Yi Ya Qiulin) established a commercial institution in Harbin, named "Qiulin Yanghang." In 1953, Qiulin Yanghang was taken over by the Chinese government, and its subsidiaries changed their names, but the name "Qiulin" was restored in 1984. Qiulin Food Factory (later renamed Qiulin Food Company) and Qiulin Confectionery Factory (later renamed Qiulin Confectionery Company) are both affiliated enterprises of Qiulin Group. Qiulin Food Factory mainly produced bread, pastries, fruit wine, and other food products. In 1997, Qiulin Confectionery Factory resumed production of Qiulin red sausage, which historically had a high reputation, with distribution by Qiulin Group and Qiulin Food Company. After several years of operation, Qiulin red sausage became one of the specialties of Harbin and gained a certain degree of recognition among the relevant public. On April 21, 1999, Qiulin Confectionery Company obtained registration of No. 1266601 "Qiulin and Device" cited trademark, designated for use on goods in Class 29, such as sausages. On July 1, 2003, Hou Yong, the legal representative of Qiulin Food Company, filed an application with the China Trademark Office for registration of the No. 3612653 "Yi Ya Qiulin" trademark, which was preliminarily approved after examination by the Trademark Office. During the opposition period, Qiulin Group filed an opposition with the Trademark Office, citing No. 1266601 "Qiulin and Device" as the cited trademark. The Trademark Office determined that the opposed trademark and the cited trademark did not constitute similar trademarks, and the opposed trademark should be registered. Qiulin Group, dissatisfied, applied for review with the TRAB. The TRAB, after examination, issued Ruling No. 4378, approving the registration of the opposed trademark. Qiulin Group, dissatisfied, filed a lawsuit. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance that the "Qiulin" character part of the cited trademark was its distinctive part, which played a primary cognitive role for consumers. The opposed trademark "Yi Ya Qiulin" completely contained the "Qiulin" character part that served as the important identifying element of the cited trademark. If the opposed trademark "Yi Ya Qiulin" were registered on goods such as canned meat, sausages, wind sausages, pork food, meat, etc., which are similar to the goods designated for the cited trademark, it would cause consumer confusion as to the source of the goods, and therefore the opposed trademark should not be permitted for registration on the above goods. The court thus vacated Ruling No. 4378 and ordered the TRAB to reissue an opposition review ruling. Hou Yong appealed. The Beijing High People's Court, after trial, sustained the first-instance judgment. Hou Yong, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on December 15, 2009, to dismiss his retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that, in this case, the prior registered cited trademark was a combination of characters and graphics, composed of the characters "Qiulin" and other graphic elements. For the relevant public, the "Qiulin" character part of the cited trademark naturally possessed an advantage in call and recognition. Furthermore, the owner of the cited trademark in this case was Qiulin Confectionery Company, whose trade name was "Qiulin." Through Qiulin Confectionery Company's use of the cited trademark, it had already acquired a certain market reputation within the province of Heilongjiang, especially in the Harbin area, and was known to the relevant public, who had become accustomed to recognizing it as the "Qiulin" trademark. The opposed trademark was the character trademark "Yi Ya Qiulin," which completely contained the "Qiulin" character part that served as the important identifying element of the cited trademark. Using the standard of attention of the relevant public, and considering that the opposed trademark was applied for registration by Hou Yong in his personal name as authorized by Qiulin Food Company, that this company and Qiulin Confectionery Company, the owner of the cited trademark, were both subordinate enterprises of the former Qiulin Company and were located in the same geographical area, if the opposed trademark were registered and used on goods such as sausages, which are similar to the goods designated for the cited trademark, it would be likely to cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or to believe there was a specific connection between them. Therefore, the opposed trademark and the cited trademark constituted similar trademarks. The formation of the "Qiulin" brand had a historical process, in which Qiulin Food Company also played an important role. However, according to the facts found, Qiulin Food Company, where Hou Yong worked, had long produced bread, fruit wine, and other products, while the opposed trademark and the cited trademark concerned Class 29 goods such as sausages. Before the application for registration of the opposed trademark, Qiulin Food Company had never produced red sausage or similar goods. In contrast, Qiulin Confectionery Company resumed production of red sausage and other products in 1997 and resumed using the "Qiulin" trademark. Through use, the "Qiulin" trademark had acquired a high degree of recognition, and this goodwill should be attributed to Qiulin Confectionery Company. Hou Yong's claim that Qiulin Food Company inherited the tradition of "Qiulin Food" and therefore had the right to register and use the opposed trademark could not be sustained.

13. Determination of trademark similarity in trademark authorization and confirmation cases where the prior trademark owner simultaneously holds a well-known trademark registered on non-similar goods and a prior registered trademark on similar goods

In trademark authorization and confirmation cases, when determining whether a disputed trademark and a cited trademark are similar, if the prior trademark owner simultaneously owns a well-known trademark registered on non-similar goods and a prior registered trademark on similar goods, there are differing views among courts on whether these two factors should be considered separately or comprehensively.

In the case of Applicant Texwood Limited (hereinafter Texwood) v. Respondent State Administration for Industry and Commerce Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and Guangdong Apple Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Guangdong Apple Company), a trademark administrative dispute [(2009) Xing Ti Zi No. 3], the Supreme People's Court pointed out that where the prior trademark owner simultaneously owns a well-known trademark registered on non-similar goods and a prior registered trademark on similar goods, not only should the disputed trademark be compared with the prior registered trademark on similar goods, but the factor of well-known trademark protection should also be considered. This judgment clarified and unified the understanding of this issue.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: On July 15, 1981, Texwood was approved by the China Trademark Office to register No. 148002 "Pingguopai" (Apple Brand) trademark, designated for use on goods in Class 25, clothing.
