On April 20, 1994, the company applied for registration of No. 813677 "texwood and Apple Device" trademark, which was approved on February 7, 1996, designated for use on goods in Class 25, including clothing, shoes, boots, hats, etc. The company also applied on April 20, 1994, and was approved on January 7, 1996, for registration of No. 805564 "texwood and Apple Device" trademark (Cited Trademark 1), designated for use on goods in Class 14, including clocks, watch cases, cuff links, tie clips, etc.; and applied on January 11, 1996, and was approved on June 21, 1997, for registration of No. 1032836 "Apple Design" trademark (Cited Trademark 2), designated for use on goods in Class 14, including jewelry, clocks and timers and their parts, watch cases, cuff links, tie clips, etc. Guangdong Apple Company (formerly Zengcheng Apple Leather Goods Co., Ltd.) applied on June 22, 1998, and was approved on January 21, 2000, for registration of No. 1355455 "Apple Design" trademark (hereinafter the disputed trademark), designated for use on goods in Class 14, including clocks, watches, watchbands, watch cases, etc. On October 23, 2000, Texwood requested the TRAB to cancel the disputed trademark, on the grounds that the disputed trademark and Cited Trademarks 1 and 2 constituted similar trademarks on similar goods, and that it maliciously copied and imitated its two well-known trademarks on denim clothing. On October 10, 2004, the TRAB issued Ruling No. [2004] 5456, finding that Texwood's "Pingguopai" and "texwood and Apple Device" trademarks had become well-known on denim clothing. The disputed trademark and Cited Trademarks 1 and 2 were both designated for use on clocks, watches, and parts and similar goods. The disputed trademark was similar in appearance to the two cited trademarks and was designated for use on identical or similar goods, likely to cause consumer confusion and misidentification, and thus all constituted similar trademarks. The TRAB ruled to cancel the registration of the disputed trademark. Guangdong Apple Company, dissatisfied, filed an administrative lawsuit. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance that Texwood's "Pingguopai" and "texwood and Apple Device" trademarks registered on denim clothing had become well-known before the application date of the disputed trademark, but the reason for the TRAB's Ruling No. 5456 to cancel the disputed trademark was not related to whether those two trademarks were well-known; Cited Trademark 1 and the disputed trademark did not constitute similar trademarks, while Cited Trademark 2 and the disputed trademark constituted similar trademarks on similar goods, and thus the court upheld the TRAB's Ruling No. 5456. Guangdong Apple Company appealed. The Beijing High People's Court found in the second instance that in its final rulings No. [2000] 2529 issued in November 2000 and No. [2001] 2510 issued in July 2001, the TRAB had determined that other disputed trademarks of Guangdong Apple Company with the same graphic design as the disputed trademark in this case, and other cited trademarks of Texwood with the same graphic design as the cited trademarks in this case, did not constitute similarity. The court of second instance held that since the TRAB had determined in those final rulings that the graphics identical to Cited Trademark 2 and the disputed trademark, respectively, did not constitute similarity, for the sake of maintaining the seriousness and uniformity of enforcement standards, it should be found that Cited Trademark 2 and the disputed trademark were not similar, and the disputed trademark should be maintained. The court of second instance vacated the first-instance judgment and the TRAB's ruling, and maintained the disputed trademark of Guangdong Apple Company. Texwood applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on December 23, 2008, to accept the retrial, and on November 11, 2009, issued a retrial judgment, vacating the second-instance judgment and sustaining the first-instance judgment and the TRAB's Ruling No. 5456.

The Supreme People's Court held in the retrial that although the TRAB in this case, having found that the disputed trademark and Cited Trademarks 1 and 2 constituted similar trademarks on identical or similar goods and should be cancelled, thus did not need to apply Article 13(2) of the Trademark Law concerning cross-class protection of well-known trademarks to cancel the disputed trademark, this did not negate Texwood's ground for cancellation that the disputed trademark constituted a reproduction or imitation of its two well-known trademarks. There is a certain degree of connection between Class 25 (clothing) and Class 14 (clocks, watches, watchbands, watch cases) in terms of sales channels and consumer groups; they are not unrelated or very weakly linked non-similar goods. Where Texwood simultaneously owned a well-known trademark registered on non-similar goods and a prior registered trademark on similar goods, not only should the disputed trademark be compared with the prior registered trademark on similar goods, but the factor of cross-class protection for well-known trademarks should also be considered. It should not be the case that a party holding both a well-known trademark and a prior registered trademark on identical or similar goods receives weaker protection than a party holding only a well-known trademark on non-similar goods. The TRAB's ruling and the first-instance judgment correctly concluded that the disputed trademark and Cited Trademark 2 constituted similar trademarks on similar goods, and that the disputed trademark should be cancelled, and these conclusions should be sustained.

14. The time limit for determining whether a trademark in dispute infringes upon another's prior rights

Article 31 of the Trademark Law provides that no trademark application for registration may infringe upon another person's existing prior rights, nor may it preemptively register, by unfair means, a trademark that has been used by another and has acquired a certain degree of influence.

In the case of Applicant Southwest Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Southwest Pharmaceutical) v. Respondent State Administration for Industry and Commerce Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and Respondent Bayer Consumer Care AG (hereinafter Bayer), a trademark administrative dispute [(2009) Xing Ti Zi No. 1], the Supreme People's Court clearly pointed out that when a people's court examines under Article 31 of the Trademark Law whether a trademark in dispute infringes upon another's prior rights, the time limit generally shall be whether the prior right existed before the application date of the trademark in dispute.

The basic facts of this case are as follows: On November 12, 1987, Southwest Pharmaceutical Company and Luoxu Company entered into a cooperative production agreement, under which Luoxu Company granted Southwest Pharmaceutical Company the right to use "Sanlitong" as the Chinese market trademark for "SARIDON," allowing Southwest Pharmaceutical Company to produce, market, sell, and wholesale this analgesic in China using Chinese raw materials. "Sanlitong" was included in the pharmaceutical standard of Sichuan Province in 1988 and in the pharmaceutical standard of Shanghai in 1995. On September 20, 2001, the National Medical Products Administration issued National Standard Publication No. 2001 GYBZ XG-013, which stipulated that, effective October 31, 2001, the local standards for "Compound Paracetamol Tablets (II)" were simultaneously discontinued, and the original drug name "Sanlitong Tablets" was retained as a former name on a transitional basis. On March 17, 1992, Southwest Pharmaceutical Company applied to register the trademark "Sanlietong," and the trademark was registered on February 28, 1993. On July 30, 1999, Luoxu Company filed a cancellation application against the "Sanlietong" trademark, on the ground that the registration infringed upon its prior rights. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board (TRAB) held that there were clear differences in the textual composition of "Sanlietong" and "Sanlitong," and that their textual meanings and functional effects were also clearly distinct, such that ordinary consumers would generally not identify them as the same trademark. Luoxu Company's claim that "Sanlietong" would be mistaken by consumers as the corresponding Chinese translation of "Saridon" and thus confused with "Sanlitong" lacked sufficient factual basis, and it could not be found that Southwest Pharmaceutical Company's registration violated the principle of good faith. By Decision No. 0675 (2005) dated April 26, 2005, the TRAB upheld the registration of the "Sanlietong" trademark. Luoxu Company, dissatisfied with this decision, filed a lawsuit. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that although the "Sanlitong" trademark was not registered in China at the time, as the Chinese translation of the English registered trademark "Saridon," it had been independently created and used for a long time by Luoxu Company, and thus constituted a trademark that Luoxu Company had used and that had acquired certain influence. "Sanlietong" and "Sanlitong" are used on identical goods, both being Western medicines, and the order and form of the characters in the two identifiers are the same; accordingly, they should be found to be similar trademarks. Southwest Pharmaceutical Company, knowing that the "Sanlitong" trademark was one used earlier by Luoxu Company and had acquired certain influence, registered the "Sanlietong" trademark, which is similar to the "Sanlitong" trademark, thereby violating the provisions of Article 31 of the Trademark Law and the principle of good faith. This constituted an act of "obtaining registration by improper means" as stipulated in Article 41 of the Trademark Law. Consequently, the court vacated TRAB Decision No. 0675. Southwest Pharmaceutical Company, dissatisfied, appealed. The Beijing High People's Court held at second instance that the disputed trademark "Sanlietong" and "Sanlitong" are similar trademarks; Southwest Pharmaceutical Company had previously entered into a cooperative production agreement with Luoxu Company and had used "Sanlitong" as a trademark or as a generic name for the pharmaceutical product under that agreement from 1987 to 1992; and Southwest Pharmaceutical Company, knowing that the "Sanlitong" mark belonged to another party, applied to register "Sanlietong," which is similar to the "Sanlitong" mark, as a trademark after the expiration of the contract between the two parties, thereby violating the principle of good faith and constituting improper registration. The court therefore dismissed the appeal and affirmed the first-instance judgment. Southwest Pharmaceutical Company, dissatisfied with that judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on January 14, 2009 to grant retrial of the case, and on May 25, 2009 rendered a retrial judgment, setting aside the judgments of first and second instance and upholding TRAB Decision No. 0675.

The Supreme People's Court found upon review that, prior to the revision of the local standard for Sanlitong on October 31, 2001, "Sanlitong" was the statutory generic name for an antipyretic and analgesic drug whose main ingredient was acetaminophen, supplemented by caffeine and isopropylantipyrine. Because both the Trademark Law and the Drug Administration Law of China prohibit the use of unregistered trademarks on pharmaceutical products, at the time when Southwest Pharmaceutical Company applied to register the "Sanlietong" trademark and when that trademark was approved for registration, "Sanlitong" could not legally be an unregistered trademark for "Sanlitong Tablets." The use of "Sanlitong" by Luoxu Company on the cooperatively produced "Sanlitong Tablets" during the period of its cooperation with Southwest Pharmaceutical Company was a labeling of the generic name of the drug in accordance with the Drug Administration Law and relevant regulations on drug labeling and package inserts, and could not be considered use of an unregistered trademark. The Supreme People's Court further held in that judgment that, since "Sanlitong" was not an unregistered trademark at the time when Southwest Pharmaceutical Company applied to register the "Sanlietong" trademark, it did not constitute the basis of rights for Luoxu Company to initiate the dispute. Although TRAB Decision No. 0675 erred in its factual finding that "Sanlitong" was an unregistered trademark of Luoxu Company, its conclusion upholding the registration of the "Sanlietong" trademark was correct and should be affirmed.
